 Medicare Premiums 2027: IRMAA Brackets and Surcharges for Parts B and D
 Do you have to pay the monthly Medicare premium surcharge in 2027? It depends.

 If you have Medicare Part B and/or Medicare Part D prescription drug coverage, you could owe a monthly surcharge based on an income-related monthly adjustment amount ( IRMAA) . High-earning Medicare beneficiaries pay this extra fee for Parts B and D in addition to standard monthly premiums if their taxable income exceeds federal thresholds. For 2027, the IRMAA income brackets widened by 3.09% across the four inflation-indexed tiers, while Part B IRMAA surcharges increased by 3.17% and Part D IRMAA surcharges increased by 6% compared to 2026.
 The Medicare surcharge in 2027 applies to beneficiaries with income exceeding $112,000 for single filers (and those married filing separately) or $224,000 for joint filers. For these high earners, total monthly Part B surcharges range from $83.70 to $502.40, while Part D surcharges range from $15.40 to $96.40.
 The IRMAA is calculated on a sliding scale with five income brackets, topping out at $500,000 for individual filers and $750,000 for married couples filing jointly. Except for the top tier, these bracket cutoffs are adjusted annually for inflation. For 2027, the inflation-adjusted brackets range from $112,000 to $500,000 for single filers and $224,000 to $750,000 for joint filers. IRMAA calculations have a two-year lag, meaning your surcharge liability in 2027 is based on your 2025 tax return.

 This surcharge applies to all Medicare and Medicare Advantage beneficiaries whose earnings cross the threshold. Because IRMAA is a strict cliff surcharge, exceeding a limit by just $1 triggers full extra payments for both Parts B and D for the entire year. Careful income planning in the years leading up to Medicare eligibility can help beneficiaries minimize or avoid these extra costs.
 Here's a look at the IRMAA and what it costs in 2027.
 The IRMAA for 2027 
 (Image credit: Getty Images) The IRMAA is a surcharge that high-income Medicare enrollees pay in addition to regular Medicare Part B and Part D premiums . This surcharge is based on your modified adjusted gross income ( MAGI) from two years prior. In other words, your 2027 IRMAA liability is determined by the MAGI reported on your 2025 tax return.
 For the IRMAA, MAGI is the sum of your adjusted gross income ( AGI) (found on line 11 of the Internal Revenue Service ( IRS ) tax filing form 1040), plus tax-exempt interest income found on line 2a of IRS Form 1040 .
 The Social Security Administration ( SSA ) uses a two-year lag because tax data from two years prior is the most recent complete information available from the IRS when annual Medicare determinations are made in the fourth quarter.
 You can calculate your total monthly Medicare costs by adding your specific IRMAA surcharge to the standard base premiums. For 2027, the standard Part B premium is $209.40 and Part D stand-alone premiums vary by plan. However, base beneficiary premium for 2027 is $41.33 and that is used by the CMS to assess the IRMAA and Part D penalties.

 Income brackets and inflation adjustments: The first four IRMAA income brackets are indexed for inflation annually. However, the top tier ($500,000 for single filers and $750,000 for joint filers) remains frozen and is not eligible for inflation adjustments until 2028 .
 How the adjustments are calculated: Under federal statute, the annual inflation adjustments for the IRMAA income thresholds are tied specifically to the Consumer Price Index for Urban Consumers ( CPI-U ). More specifically, the formula measures the percentage increase in the average CPI-U over the 12 months ending in August of the current year compared to the average CPI-U for the preceding 12 months
 How you pay your IRMAA surcharges
 (Image credit: Getty Images) How you pay your IRMAA fees depends primarily on whether you are currently collecting Social Security benefits:
 Direct deduction from Social Security: If you receive Social Security benefits, both your standard Part B premium and your Part B/Part D IRMAA surcharges are automatically withheld from your monthly benefit check
 Billed directly by Medicare (CMS-500): If you are on Medicare but haven't started taking Social Security yet, you will receive a direct quarterly bill from Medicare for your premiums and Part B IRMAA surcharges . You can pay online via your secure Medicare.gov accoun t , sign up for free automatic ACH withdrawals via Medicare Easy Medicare Premium Collection Center
PO Box 790355
St. Louis, MO 63179-0355
 Part D IRMAA payments: Even if your underlying Part D plan premium is billed through a private insurer (or deducted from your benefit), the Part D IRMAA surcharge is paid directly to Medicare every month — not to your Part D insurance carrier
 Types of income that trigger the IRMAA
 (Image credit: Getty Images) The Medicare surcharge isn't based on your taxable income alone — it is calculated using your Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI).
 In simple terms, for IRMAA purposes, your MAGI is your AGI from Form 1040 plus specific tax-exempt add-backs. Most sources of taxable income — along with a few non-taxable exceptions — count toward this total:
 Wages, self-employment income, and business profits:  Standard earned income from working or running a business
 Taxable pensions and annuity distributions:  Regular payouts from employer-sponsored pension plans or commercial annuities
 Traditional IRA and 401(k) distributions:  Withdrawals from tax-deferred retirement accounts — including mandatory Required Minimum Distributions (RMDs) — are treated as ordinary income
 Capital gains and dividends:  Realized gains from selling stocks, mutual funds, real estate, or other taxable assets, as well as taxable dividend payouts
 Tax-exempt municipal bond interest:  A common trap for retirees. Interest earned from municipal bonds is tax-free on your federal return, but it  must be added back  to calculate your MAGI for Medicare surcharges
 Social Security benefits:  Up to 85% of your Social Security benefits can be taxable — and that taxable portion counts directly toward your MAGI
 Other tax-exempt add-backs:  Excluded U.S. Savings Bond interest used for higher education, as well as foreign earned income and non-taxable income from U.S. territories
 Reminder : Roth IRA withdrawals, qualified HSA distributions, and life insurance proceeds do not count toward your MAGI.
 Because your 2027 IRMAA is tied strictly to the MAGI reported on your 2025 tax return, unexpected spike years — such as selling a home, taking a large lump-sum IRA withdrawal, or executing a massive Roth conversion — can trigger an unexpected bump in your Medicare premiums two years down the line.

 How to appeal the IRMAA
 (Image credit: Getty Images) Appealing an IRMAA determination depends on whether the SSA used incorrect data or whether your income dropped due to a major life change.
 If the SSA used the wrong tax year data or miscalculated your MAGI entirely (and no life-changing event occurred), you file a standard request for reconsideration (non-medical) through Form SSA-561 within 60 days of receiving your initial IRMAA determination notice .
 To request a reduction in your surcharge based on a drop in income, you must file Form SSA-44 (Medicare Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount – Life-Changing Event).
 Qualifying life-changing events: The SSA only accepts requests if your income dropped because of one of eight specific events:
 Work stoppage or reduction (retirement or cutting hours — the most common trigger)
 Marriage
 Death of a spouse
 Divorce or annulment
 Loss of income-producing property (due to disaster or theft)
 Loss or reduction of pension income
 Employer settlement payment
 Reminder : Voluntary one-time spikes — like a large Roth conversion, capital gains from selling a home, or standard investment fluctuations — do not qualify.
 How to file an appeal:
 Complete Form SSA-44: Check your qualifying event, provide the date it occurred, and enter your estimated current-year MAGI. You can view and/or download the form on the SSA's website.
 Gather proof: Attach evidence of the event (e.g., a retirement letter from an employer, death certificate or divorce decree) plus proof of your lower income, such as a signed tax return or recent pay stubs.
 Submit: Upload the form and documents securely via your online Social Security account , or mail, fax, or bring it to a local SSA office.
 If filing online isn't an option, call 1-800-772-1213 ("TTY" number, 1-800-325-0778) and explain that you don't want to use the online appeal process but you do want to appeal the decision made in your case. Representatives can send you the form or schedule an appointment at a local SSA office . Help is available Monday through Friday from 7 am to 7 pm.
